questions.question: A minimization problem has finite optimal value. Here $z^*$ is the optimal value, $z_H$ the value of a feasible solution and $z_R$ the optimal value of a relaxation with the same objective. Which ordering always holds?
options: $z_H\le z^*\le z_R$
$z_R\le z^*\le z_H$
$z^*\le z_R\le z_H$
$z_R\le z_H\le z^*$

questions.question: For a cost-minimization problem, an analyst drops two constraints and also replaces the cost function by a simpler one, then solves this modified problem to optimality and obtains the value 90. Can 90 serve as a lower bound on the original optimal cost?
options: Yes; dropping constraints makes the value a lower bound whatever the objective is.
Yes, provided the simpler cost function is linear like the original one.
No; a lower bound can only come from a feasible solution of the original problem.
No; the bound needs a relaxation that keeps the original cost function unchanged.

questions.question: For a cost-minimization problem, a heuristic returns a feasible plan. What kind of bound does its cost give on the optimal cost?
options: A lower bound: the optimum costs at least this much.
The exact optimal cost, since the plan is feasible.
An upper bound: the optimum costs at most this much.
No bound, since a heuristic is not guaranteed optimal.

questions.question: In a minimization problem, a feasible plan costs 75 and a relaxation with the same objective has optimal value 75. What follows?
options: The plan is optimal, and the optimal cost is 75.
The optimal cost is somewhere between 0 and 75.
The plan is optimal only if the relaxed optimizer is feasible.
The optimal cost is below 75, as the relaxation was solved.

questions.question: For a delivery-route problem that minimizes total miles, a found route is 214 miles long and a relaxation has optimal value 202 miles. At most how many miles could a better route still save compared with the 214-mile route?
options: 202 miles
214 miles
30 miles
12 miles

questions.question: In a profit-maximization problem, a heuristic plan earns 150 and a relaxation with the same objective has optimal value 170. What is known about the maximum profit $z^*$?
options: At least 170, with no upper limit
Exactly 160, the midpoint of the two
From 150 up to 170, both included
At most 150, with no lower limit

questions.question: For a minimization problem, a heuristic plan costs $z_H=120$ and a relaxation has optimal value $z_R=100$; the optimal cost is $z^*$. What does $z_H-z^*\le z_H-z_R$ guarantee?
options: The plan costs at most 20 more than the optimum.
The plan costs exactly 20 more than the optimum.
The plan costs at least 20 more than the optimum.
The plan costs at most 20 less than the optimum.

questions.question: For a minimization problem, $z^*$ is the optimal value, $z_H$ the value of a feasible solution and $z_R$ the optimal value of a relaxation with the same objective. Which reasons give the two inequalities $z_R\le z^*$ and $z^*\le z_H$?
options: The optimum stays feasible in the relaxation; the heuristic's plan is feasible.
The relaxed optimizer is feasible for the original; the heuristic's plan is feasible.
The relaxation has fewer variables; the heuristic always overestimates.
The relaxed optimizer is feasible; the heuristic's plan is near-optimal.

questions.question: For a minimization problem, the current bounds are a relaxation value 50 and a feasible cost 55. Which new result could narrow this interval?
options: Dropping more constraints from the relaxation
Finding a feasible plan that costs 58
Finding a feasible plan that costs 53
A relaxed-feasible solution costing 52

questions.question: For a minimization problem, a heuristic plan costs 110 and the relaxation's optimal value is 100. Does the positive gap show that the heuristic plan is not optimal?
options: Yes; a positive gap means a cheaper feasible plan exists.
Yes; an optimal plan would always cost exactly 100.
No; the plan may be optimal while the relaxation is loose.
No; it shows instead that the relaxation was solved wrongly.

questions.question: For one minimization problem, three heuristics give feasible plans costing 58, 61 and 55, and two different relaxations have optimal values 47 and 50. What is the narrowest interval for the optimal cost these values justify?
options: From 47 to 61
From 50 to 61
From 47 to 55
From 50 to 55

questions.question: For a mileage-minimizing delivery problem, the best known route is 214 miles and a relaxation gave 202. Putting one dropped restriction back, so that the relaxation still contains every allowed route, raises the relaxed optimal value to 208. What can now be said?
options: The 214-mile route is within 6 miles of the optimum.
The 214-mile route is still only known to be within 12 miles.
The optimal mileage is now known to be exactly 208.
The optimum is at least 214, since the bound rose.

questions.question: Minimize $2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\ge4$, $x_1\le2$ and $x_1,x_2\ge0$, with optimal value $z^*$. The plan $(1,3)$ is feasible, and dropping $x_1\le2$ gives a relaxation with optimal value 8. Which interval do these two facts give?

For a minimization problem, a heuristic plan costs 100. A solver for a relaxation (with the same objective) is stopped early and returns a relaxed-feasible solution costing 95, without proving it optimal for the relaxation. An analyst concludes that the heuristic is within 5 of optimal. Is this justified?
options: Yes; the relaxation always gives a lower bound on the optimum.
No; 95 merely bounds the relaxed optimum from above, not below.
Yes; the optimal cost must lie between 95 and 100 in any case.
No; the heuristic plan must be optimal, since 100 exceeds 95.

questions.question: In a profit-maximization problem, a heuristic plan earns 170. An analyst builds a model that is supposed to be a relaxation and finds its optimal value 160. What follows?
options: The maximum profit lies between 160 and 170.
The heuristic plan is optimal, earning profit 170.
The maximum profit is at most 160 after all.
The model cannot be a valid relaxation here.
